sourceCheck: Verified on 2026-10-08. Opened https://www.mongodb.com/docs/ and https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/release-notes/ first, followed by https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/release-notes/9.0/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/release-notes/9.0-compatibility/ and https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongodb-versions/. The release index identifies Current Stable Release as 9.0-series, and the manual selector shows 9.0 (Current). The deck remains pinned to MongoDB Server 9.0. Drivers, mongosh and Database Tools have independent version numbers; driver serialization defaults and driver-specific retries are excluded. Binary upgrades and FCV changes are separate operations. Transactions require replica sets or sharded clusters; their documented historical minimum FCVs are 4.0 and 4.2 respectively. No additional FCV prerequisite is stated in the selected references for constraint validation, the 9.0 operation memory limit, concurrent multikey query interruption or external-client transaction concurrency limits. Sharded lookup, merge, routing and uniqueness facts will identify their topology. Ordinary unsharded collections are the default; Atlas Infinite, managed administration, views, capped collections and time series collections are excluded. Confirmed changes and traps: MongoDB 9.0 constraint validation checks existing documents when enabled, requires error or errorAndLog, and locks validator rules; strict does not retroactively scan existing documents. Scalar null equality still matches missing fields; the 8.0 change concerns legacy BSON undefined, which is excluded. find projections accept aggregation expressions. Pipeline updates permit a restricted stage subset. Ordered inserts retain earlier successful writes outside transactions. MongoDB 9.0 introduces a combined per-operation memory limit separate from stage limits and spilling. The 9.0 release notes reverse the 8.0 deprecation of $where, $function and $accumulator through a WebAssembly engine; server-side JavaScript remains outside the deck. A concurrent multikey transition can interrupt a referencing query with QueryKilledError in 9.0. ESR is a guideline, and selective ranges can justify ERS; changing numeric $in thresholds are excluded. Text indexes remain supported; Search and Vector Search are excluded. Partial uniqueness applies to the indexed subset, and TTL deletion runs in background work. The 9.0 transaction concurrency limit concerns external clients and a configured server-wide limit; numeric defaults are excluded. Majority write acknowledgment concerns durable oplog recording, while secondary application remains asynchronous. Snapshot reads include supported operations outside transactions. Causal read-your-writes requires a causally consistent session with majority read and write concerns. Current balancing considers collection data amounts. Legacy automatic splitting stopped in 6.0.3 and autosplit toggles have no effect; migration-related range splitting remains possible. Config shards can store application data, and documented writes can change non-_id shard-key values. Excluded contradictory or stale material: updateOne's claim that aggregation $set does not modify existing values; old transaction and causal summaries equating majority acknowledgment with secondary application; Atlas-only Search wording in the $text reference; namespace-file details in referencing guidance; an inconsistent multikey whole-array example; routing summaries requiring shard key or _id for modern single-document writes; conflicting initial hashed chunk counts; and an old exact-FCV note on refineCollectionShardKey. Operator-specific references resolve selected facts. Separate $ne missing-field testing is omitted because the exclusion/missing lesson is owned by the $nin card. Language-picker tutorial shells and failed Markdown fetches supply no card evidence. cards.statement: A MongoDB document field can hold an embedded document or an array.
cards.explanation: A BSON field can contain another document or an array, letting one record carry nested values.

cards.statement: MongoDB stores a document as plain JSON text on the server.
cards.explanation: MongoDB stores BSON documents. BSON is a binary format with value types beyond those available in plain JSON.
cards.misconception: MongoDB persists the same plain JSON text used to display a record.

cards.statement: Canonical Extended JSON uses $numberLong for a BSON long whose value also fits in int.
cards.explanation: Canonical Extended JSON preserves the BSON long type through the $numberLong wrapper, even for small values.

cards.statement: BSON stores int and long values as separate numeric types.
cards.explanation: BSON int stores a 32-bit integer, while BSON long stores a 64-bit integer. They remain distinct stored types.

cards.statement: Decimal128('0.1') stores a binary approximation of the decimal value.
cards.explanation: Decimal128('0.1') represents that decimal exactly. Decimal128 uses decimal floating point for this value.
cards.misconception: Decimal128 approximates decimal fractions using the same binary representation as double.

cards.statement: BSON Date automatically retains the original timezone offset of a stored instant.
cards.explanation: BSON Date stores an instant as milliseconds relative to the Unix epoch. The stored value contains no original timezone offset.
cards.misconception: BSON Date retains the timezone offset from its input.

cards.statement: BSON Timestamp is the recommended type for application event dates.
cards.explanation: MongoDB reserves BSON Timestamp primarily for internal operations. Its documentation recommends BSON Date for ordinary application dates.
cards.misconception: BSON Timestamp is the preferred application date type.

cards.statement: ObjectId() with no argument embeds the time when the value is generated.
cards.explanation: ObjectId() generates a value whose timestamp component records its creation time.

cards.statement: Sorting generated ObjectId values puts them in their exact creation order.
cards.explanation: ObjectId ordering is approximate. Values generated in the same second and differences between client clocks prevent exact creation ordering.
cards.misconception: ObjectId sorting guarantees exact chronological creation order.

cards.statement: MongoDB can store a UUID as BSON binary data with a UUID subtype.
cards.explanation: BSON binary values carry a subtype. The UUID subtype identifies binary data that represents a UUID.

cards.statement: MongoDB applies its BSON size limit to the complete document, including embedded contents.
cards.explanation: MongoDB's BSON document limit applies to the entire enclosing record; embedded documents and arrays contribute to its size.

cards.statement: MongoDB can store a field name containing an embedded null character.
cards.explanation: MongoDB excludes the null character from BSON field names.
cards.misconception: A BSON field name may contain a null character.

cards.statement: insertOne() creates an ordinary collection when its target collection is absent.
cards.explanation: An insert into a collection that does not exist causes MongoDB to create the ordinary collection implicitly.

cards.statement: db.createCollection() can attach a validator while creating an ordinary collection.
cards.explanation: The validator option of db.createCollection() installs validation rules at collection creation.

cards.statement: MongoDB uses the first inserted document to fix field types for later documents in that collection.
cards.explanation: Documents in a collection may use different fields and BSON types. The first insert does not establish a collection-wide field-type contract.
cards.misconception: The first inserted document determines the schema for later inserts.

cards.statement: A $jsonSchema validator makes a field mandatory when its properties entry specifies bsonType.
cards.explanation: A $jsonSchema properties rule constrains a field when it is present. The required array separately specifies mandatory fields.
cards.misconception: Specifying bsonType under properties also requires the field to exist.

cards.statement: MongoDB checks existing documents when an administrator enables validationLevel: 'strict'.
cards.explanation: Enabling strict validation does not retroactively scan existing documents for compliance. It checks documents as relevant writes occur.
cards.misconception: The strict level retroactively validates existing collection data.

source.title: Specify Validation Level for Existing Documents

cards.statement: With validationLevel: 'moderate', MongoDB skips validation for updates to existing invalid documents.
cards.explanation: The moderate level exempts updates to documents that already violate the validator from its validation checks.

source.title: Specify Validation Level for Existing Documents

cards.statement: In MongoDB 9.0, MongoDB locks the validator rules while validationLevel is 'constraint'.
cards.explanation: At the constraint level, MongoDB prevents changes to validator rules. Lower the level before modifying those rules.
cards.volatilityNote: MongoDB 9.0 introduces this validation level; its restrictions may evolve in later releases.

source.title: Specify Validation Level for Existing Documents

cards.statement: With validationLevel: 'strict' and validationAction: 'warn', MongoDB rejects an invalid insert.
cards.explanation: With strict validation and validationAction: 'warn', MongoDB permits the invalid insert and logs the violation.
cards.misconception: The warn action rejects writes that fail the validator.

source.title: Choose How to Handle Invalid Documents

cards.statement: MongoDB clients can generate an ObjectId for _id before sending an insert.
cards.explanation: MongoDB clients commonly generate _id before sending an insert. If a received document omits _id, mongod generates it.

cards.statement: A document can use a BSON array as its _id value.
cards.explanation: MongoDB excludes arrays from the permitted BSON types for _id.
cards.misconception: Any BSON value, including an array, is a valid _id.

cards.statement: An update can change _id while retaining the same stored document.
cards.explanation: The _id value of a stored document is immutable. Updating that document retains its identifier.
cards.misconception: An update can rename the identity of an existing document.

cards.statement: MongoDB automatically creates a unique _id index on an ordinary unsharded collection.
cards.explanation: An ordinary unsharded collection receives its unique _id index at creation, enforcing uniqueness of its document identifiers.

cards.statement: insertOne() returns the inserted document's _id in its insertedId result field.
cards.explanation: The insertOne() result reports the newly inserted identifier through insertedId.

cards.statement: By default, insertMany() stops processing later documents after a duplicate key error.
cards.explanation: insertMany() uses ordered: true by default. A duplicate key error stops the remaining inserts in that ordered batch.

cards.statement: Outside a transaction, ordered insertMany() rolls back earlier inserts after a duplicate key error.
cards.explanation: Outside a transaction, successful inserts before an ordered insertMany() error remain stored. The failure does not undo them.
cards.misconception: Ordered insertion gives the entire batch rollback behavior.

cards.statement: insertMany() with ordered: false preserves the input order of successful inserts.
cards.explanation: For ordered: false, mongod may reorder insert operations. The application has no input-order guarantee.
cards.misconception: Unordered insertion continues after errors while guaranteeing input order.

cards.statement: db.collection.findOne() returns a cursor positioned at its first matching document.
cards.explanation: findOne() returns a matching document itself, rather than a cursor for iterating matches.
cards.misconception: findOne() returns a single-result cursor.

cards.statement: db.collection.findOne() returns null when its filter matches zero documents.
cards.explanation: A findOne() query with zero matches produces null, so callers can check for the absent result.

cards.statement: MongoDB sends results from a find() cursor in batches as the client consumes them.
cards.explanation: A find() cursor delivers results in batches; iterating it retrieves further results as needed.

cards.statement: MongoDB preserves insertion order among documents with equal cursor.sort() keys.
cards.explanation: MongoDB leaves the order of documents tied on sort keys unspecified. Their relative insertion order supplies no stable tie-breaker.
cards.misconception: Equal sort keys retain insertion order.

cards.statement: MongoDB's find().limit(5) bounds the total returned documents across cursor batches.
cards.explanation: The cursor limit bounds the total query result, rather than setting a fresh allowance for each batch.

cards.statement: Chaining limit() before skip() makes MongoDB apply the limit before the skip.
cards.explanation: MongoDB applies skip before limit when the cursor methods are chained. Reversing their method-call order leaves that behavior unchanged.
cards.misconception: The order of skip() and limit() calls determines their execution order.

cards.statement: db.collection.deleteOne({}) chooses the document with the smallest _id in a nonempty collection.
cards.explanation: deleteOne({}) removes the first document selected by the operation. Its empty filter does not request ordering by _id.
cards.misconception: An empty deleteOne() filter selects the minimum _id.

cards.statement: db.collection.deleteMany({}) leaves an ordinary collection's index definitions in place.
cards.explanation: Document deletion keeps the collection's index definitions, including when deleteMany({}) removes its data.

cards.statement: MongoDB treats {state: 'ready'} like {state: {$eq: 'ready'}} in a query filter.
cards.explanation: For a scalar string, {state: 'ready'} is the equality shorthand for {state: {$eq: 'ready'}}.

cards.statement: Query {score: {$gt: 5}} treats stored strings such as '9' as numeric scores.
cards.explanation: A numeric query comparison uses BSON type bracketing. A stored string '9' is not converted to a number for {score: {$gt: 5}}.
cards.misconception: Comparison query predicates coerce numeric-looking strings to numbers.

cards.statement: MongoDB combines {active: true, region: 'eu'} as an implicit $and query.
cards.explanation: The filter {active: true, region: 'eu'} requires both field conditions to match; MongoDB supplies an implicit AND.

cards.statement: A matching first $or clause protects a query from errors in its later clauses.
cards.explanation: MongoDB may evaluate an error-producing later $or clause even when the first clause matches. Clause order supplies no short-circuit safety guarantee.
cards.misconception: A successful $or clause prevents evaluation errors in later clauses.

cards.statement: Query {$nor: [{state: 'closed'}, {archived: true}]} matches {state: 'open', archived: false}.
cards.explanation: The $nor filter excludes state: 'closed' and archived: true. A document with state: 'open' and archived: false satisfies it.

cards.statement: The $in query predicate can contain $regex operator expressions in its value list.
cards.explanation: $in accepts regular expression literals such as /^ada/. It rejects nested $regex operator expressions as list items.
cards.misconception: $in accepts $regex operator documents wherever it accepts regex literals.

cards.statement: Query {state: {$nin: ['open']}} also matches documents where the state field is missing.
cards.explanation: The $nin query for ['open'] selects documents missing the state field as well as documents with an eligible value outside that list.

cards.statement: Query {status: null} restricts matching documents to those with a present status field.
cards.explanation: The scalar query {status: null} matches a null status value or a missing status field.
cards.misconception: Equality to null implies that the tested field exists.

cards.statement: Query {status: {$exists: true}} filters out documents whose status value is null.
cards.explanation: $exists: true tests field presence and includes a present field whose value is null.
cards.misconception: Field existence implies that the field has a non-null value.

cards.statement: Query {score: {$type: 'number'}} matches a BSON Decimal128 value such as Decimal128('42').
cards.explanation: The query $type alias 'number' includes BSON decimal values, so it matches a Decimal128 score.

cards.statement: Query {name: {$regex: '^ada'}} matches 'Ada' with the default $regex options.
cards.explanation: $regex matching is case-sensitive by default. The pattern '^ada' needs case-insensitive matching to select 'Ada'.
cards.misconception: Query $regex uses case-insensitive matching by default.

cards.statement: Query {$expr: {$gt: ['$spent', '$budget']}} compares two fields of the same document.
cards.explanation: Inside query $expr, '$spent' and '$budget' read fields from the same document for the comparison.
